sentences.text: Torvosaurus tanneri measured around 9 meters long and weighed approximately 2 to 2.4 metric tons, making it one of the largest terrestrial carnivores in Late Jurassic North America.
Later research suggests adults could reach 9 to 11 meters in length and weigh up to 2 to 4.4 metric tons.
This animal was a large, robust, bipedal carnivore that could grow to nearly 10 meters in length.
It is considered an enormous predator with an estimated maximum body length of 10 meters and a mass of 4 to 5 tonnes for both T. tanneri and T. gurneyi.
The skull featured fused interdental plates within the jaw structure.
A specimen nicknamed 'Elvis' stands as the most complete Torvosaurus specimen found to date.
Torvosaurus gurneyi holds the title of the largest named theropod from Europe, although a Spanish vertebra from the Vega Formation is about 15% larger.
The species gurneyi possesses the largest teeth of any theropod discovered in the Lourinhã Formation.
Embryos of this genus found in Portugal represent the only known basal theropod embryos.
The first remains referable to Torvosaurus were discovered in 1899 by Elmer Riggs in the Freeze-out Hills of southeastern Wyoming.
A gigantic theropod thumb claw was discovered in 1971 by Vivian Jones at the Calico Gulch Quarry in Moffat County, Colorado.
The genus Torvosaurus was named by Peter Malcolm Galton and James Alvin Jensen in 1979.
The type species Torvosaurus tanneri was formally named in 1979.
The specific name tanneri honors Nathan Eldon Tanner, a first counselor in the First Presidency of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.
The type specimen of Torvosaurus tanneri is housed in the collection of Brigham Young University in Provo, Utah.
The animal may have been specialized in opening and dismembering exceptionally large sauropod carcasses due to its large skull, teeth, and powerful body.
Torvosaurus and Ceratosaurus likely preferred waterways and had lower, sinuous bodies suited for forest and underbrush terrain.
Evidence suggests Allosaurus was a potential food item for other carnivores, indicated by bite marks on its pubic foot likely made by Ceratosaurus or Torvosaurus.
Eggs with and without embryos referred to Torvosaurus were reported from Portugal in 2013 and 2014.
The discovery of Torvosaurus eggs supports the idea that large theropod dinosaurs were oviparous.
This specimen represents the first evidence of a single-layered eggshell in theropod dinosaurs.
The non-perturbed taphonomic environment and low-energy geological context corroborate that the eggs were buried for incubation.
All documented Torvosaurus specimens from the Morrison Formation are likely adult individuals of similar size.
Torvosaurus may have experienced Type B1 population survival, characterized by increased mortality after reaching sexual maturity, as seen in other dinosaurs.
All documented Torvosaurus specimens from the Morrison Formation appear to be similarly sized adult individuals, though the lack of immature individuals may be due to various factors.
The highly porous eggshells of Torvosaurus indicate that the eggs were buried in the substrate for incubation, similar to modern sea turtles.
Torvosaurus was first classified as a megalosaurid in 1979, a classification that remains the current consensus.
Torvosaurus is classified in the family Megalosauridae.
Most researchers now consider Edmarka rex and the informal name Brontoraptor to be junior synonyms of Torvosaurus tanneri.
Torvosaurus lived during the Middle to Late Jurassic periods, specifically from the Callovian to Tithonian ages.
Evidence suggests megalosaurines may have originated in Europe or that Europe served as a biogeographical hub for them from the Middle to early Late Jurassic.
It is debated whether teeth from Tanzania and Uruguay belong to Torvosaurus, as some researchers consider them undiagnostic and similar to other theropods like carcharodontosaurids.
One describer of Torvosaurus gurneyi argued that giant vertebrae from the Vega Formation likely belong to T. gurneyi, though this is debated.
It is debated whether the lower number of maxillary teeth in Torvosaurus gurneyi is a real distinction or an artifact of preservation, as the exact count remains unknown.
